title: Crystal model and simulation workflow
caption: **Figure 1. Crystal model and simulation workflow.** (a) Conventional FCC copper cell, with eight corner sites and six face-center sites contributing four effective atoms per cell. (b) Periodic 10 × 10 × 10 conventional-cell model containing 4,000 atoms; the displayed lattice is a schematic representation rather than an atom-count-resolved trajectory snapshot. (c) Model preparation, independently initialized NPT calculations, the 200 ps equilibration and 500 ps production segments, and expansion analysis. Structural illustrations are not to scale.

title: Thermal expansion and lattice fluctuations
caption: **Figure 2. Mean thermal expansion, lattice fluctuations, and repeat-resolved volume changes of periodic single-crystal copper.** (a) Mean lattice parameter from three independently initialized production trajectories at each temperature. Error bars are two-sided 95% Student-t confidence intervals with two degrees of freedom and may be smaller than the markers. Open squares, diamonds, and triangles show repeats r1, r2, and r3, respectively; fixed horizontal offsets of −12, 0, and +12 K are used only for visibility, without changing their lattice-parameter values. Filled circles are plotted at the actual temperatures, and connecting lines are guides to the eye. (b) Half-violin densities and boxplots summarize production-sample fluctuations after subtracting each trajectory's own mean lattice parameter and pooling the three centered trajectories per temperature. Densities use Scott's bandwidth rule and are displayed only over the observed ranges. Violin widths are scaled to a common maximum and do not encode sample size. Boxes show the interquartile range and median; whiskers reach the most extreme observations within 1.5 interquartile ranges. Boxplot outlier symbols are omitted; the density display retains the full observed range. These correlated samples describe fluctuations, not independent replicate measurements or confidence intervals. (c) Directly averaged volumes normalized to each repeat's own 300 K volume, with values in percent. The 300 K zeros follow from normalization. Blue-to-green marker and distribution colors identify temperature in (a,b), whereas the continuous teal scale in (c) encodes volume change. All panels exclude the first 200 ps and use the subsequent 500 ps production segment.

title: Comparison with the NIST reference
caption: **Figure 3. Comparison of copper thermal expansion predicted by the Mishin EAM1 potential with the revised NIST SRM 736 reference.** (a) Linear expansion relative to 300 K, with MD means obtained from three independently initialized production trajectories per temperature. (b) Mean MD-minus-NIST residuals in ppm, with temperature increasing upward. (c) Engineering interval-average coefficients, calculated for each MD repeat as $\bar\alpha_r=[\bar a_r(800\,\mathrm{K})/\bar a_r(300\,\mathrm{K})-1]/(500\,\mathrm{K})$ and then averaged. Error bars in all panels are two-sided 95% Student-t confidence intervals with two degrees of freedom and describe MD sampling variability only; reference uncertainty has not been propagated, and no reference interval is implied to be zero. MD strains are normalized separately to each repeat's own 300 K mean. NIST fractional length changes relative to 293 K are converted to the 300 K reference using the revised certificate dated 7 October 1990, p. 1. The coincident curves and zero residual with zero interval at 300 K follow from normalization, not independent validation. In (c), open squares, diamonds, and triangles represent r1, r2, and r3, with vertical category offsets of −0.14, 0, and +0.14 for visibility only; coefficient values are not shifted. Temperature colors are consistent between (a) and (b). Connecting lines are guides to the eye, and some intervals may be smaller than the markers. All MD averages exclude 200 ps of equilibration and use the subsequent 500 ps production segment.

title: Sensitivity to simulation settings
caption: **Figure 4. Sensitivity to simulation settings.** (a) Baseline and modified settings, with colored cells identifying the parameters changed from the baseline. Unchanged values use neutral backgrounds; colors identify conditions and are not a numerical scale across unlike units. (b) Relative changes in the engineering 300–800 K average linear expansion coefficient, calculated as $100(\bar\alpha_{\mathrm{condition}}/\bar\alpha_{\mathrm{baseline},r1}-1)$. Every comparison uses production repeat r1 at 300 and 800 K as the baseline, rather than the three-repeat mean. Each modified condition contains one trajectory at each endpoint, and no independent-repeat uncertainty intervals are available for these checks. The horizontal axis is expanded to resolve small changes; the prespecified ±2% practical sensitivity target lies outside the displayed range. Passing these limited checks supports robustness under the tested changes, not universal convergence or an exact bound on numerical error.

title: Recorded trajectory diagnostics
caption: **Figure 5. Recorded trajectory diagnostics for periodic single-crystal copper.** (a) Separate 3D volume trajectories for production repeat r1 at six target temperatures. Volume changes are normalized to the single common denominator $\bar V_{300,r1}=47\,908.5892\,\text{Å}^3$, averaged over 200 < time ≤ 700 ps. Target temperature labels separate simulation conditions rather than instantaneous temperatures. Gray traces indicate the first 200 ps; colored traces indicate the following production segment, with the recorded 200 ps boundary point retained for visual line continuity only. The faint plane marks 200 ps and is not an interpolated data surface. (b–d) Recorded endpoint r1 trajectories at 300 and 800 K: actual temperature minus target temperature, instantaneous pressure (1 bar = 10⁻⁴ GPa), and potential energy per atom minus that trajectory's own production mean. Light traces show every recorded point, including step 0; darker solid (300 K) and dashed (800 K) traces show trailing 50-record means (5 ps at the 0.1 ps recording interval), reset at the production boundary with shorter startup windows. These means are display aids only. No temporal decimation, detrending, variance rescaling, or temperature interpolation is used. All curves represent individual r1 trajectories, not averages over three repeats. Energy centering sets the production mean to zero by construction. The plots provide diagnostic evidence but do not alone prove complete equilibration or independent sampling; fluctuations are not confidence intervals.

title: Sensitivity to statistical block duration
caption: **Figure 6. Sensitivity of lattice-parameter standard-error estimates to statistical block duration.** All 24 completed trajectories are analyzed separately: 18 production trajectories followed by six endpoint validation trajectories, with groups separated in (a). Each standard error is the sample standard deviation of nonoverlapping block means divided by the square root of the complete-block count. (a) Ratios to each trajectory's own 20 ps standard error, encoded by a shared symmetric $\log_2$ ratio color scale; colorbar labels show the corresponding ratios. The copper outline marks the 20 ps column, whose ratio of one follows from normalization. Lavender and teal indicate ratios below and above one, not pass/fail classifications. (b) Absolute standard errors for production repeat r1 at 300 and 800 K; circles and triangles identify the two temperatures, open rings highlight 20 and 50 ps, and connecting segments are guides to the eye on the logarithmic duration axis. (c) Paired 20 and 50 ps estimates for all trajectories, with equal axes and a 1:1 reference line. Colors identify temperature; filled circles and open diamonds identify production and validation trajectories. The annotated range is the observed range of ratios, not a confidence interval. Standard trajectories use 500 ps after 200 ps equilibration; long-duration checks use 1,000 ps after 1,000 ps equilibration. Longer blocks reduce the number of available block means and can increase variability in the estimated error. Limited sensitivity within these tested block durations does not establish complete independence, universal convergence, or the absence of slower correlations.
